title: Medical governance: Classification cannot replace lifecycle oversight
desc: Combines regulatory boundaries, planned modification, representative testing and public records without treating inventories as complete clinical evidence.

kps.k: Medical-AI governance combines regulatory classification, independent professional review and lifecycle oversight rather than treating all AI alike.
kps.d: FDA’s PCCP guidance applies to AI software functions that qualify as medical devices and preserves statutory exclusions. Automated Decision Support Technologies and the Legal Profession reproduces statutory language requiring clinicians to be able to independently review the basis of recommendations rather than rely primarily on them. Together, these materials make software purpose and the clinician’s role central to the applicable governance framework; they do not establish a corresponding regulatory regime for legal AI.

kps.k: Regulatory boundaries influence development choices, but classification does not settle what oversight is appropriate.
kps.d: Humans in the Loop reports unresolved AI/ML clinical decision-support questions in two draft FDA guidance documents and describes Duke’s work with officials to classify Sepsis Watch as clinical decision support rather than a diagnostic device. Separately, Automated Decision Support Technologies and the Legal Profession reports Evans and Whicher’s argument for enhanced oversight even when use falls outside research under the Common Rule. Their proposal includes conditions of use, ongoing data-quality monitoring, algorithm validation and patient-data protection. These accounts expose a tension between formal regulatory categories and proposed safeguards, not a direct disagreement about the same rule. The draft-guidance account does not establish whether later guidance resolved those uncertainties.

kps.k: FDA proposes planned, risk-managed modification as a way to accommodate iterative AI development while maintaining oversight.
kps.d: Predetermined change control plans place anticipated changes within marketing submissions and a total-product-lifecycle approach grounded in benefit-risk assessment and modification risk management. The guidance addresses establishing, implementing and modifying plans. It remains nonbinding and permits alternatives that satisfy applicable law. FDA presents learning from real-world data and improved model performance as potential benefits, not demonstrated clinical outcomes; its report of increasing submissions supplies no counts in these excerpts.

qs.q: To support the iterative development of AI-DSFs, and as part of the proposed framework presented in the 2019 discussion paper, FDA described a “Predetermined Change Control Plan” that could be included in a marketing submission for an AI/ML-based device.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The ideas delineated in the 2019 discussion paper and further described in this guidance leveraged practices from our premarket programs and relied on the International Medical Device Regulators Forum’s risk categorization principles, 6 the FDA’s benefit-risk framework, 7 risk management principles described in the Device Modifications guidances, 8 and a total product lifecycle approach.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Credible oversight requires representative data and clear distinctions between model development and performance testing.
kps.d: FDA recommends training data that represent intended populations and environments, including relevant demographic and disease characteristics. It places tuning within training and before testing, uses test data to characterize device performance, and explicitly rejects using validation as a synonym for tuning. For manufacturers, the practical implication is to distinguish these activities in development documentation rather than treat tuning results as testing evidence. These recommendations specify an assurance process; the excerpts do not measure its effectiveness.

kps.k: Public authorization records improve visibility but cannot serve as a complete census or a full account of clinical evidence.
kps.d: FDA says listed devices met applicable premarket requirements, including review of safety, effectiveness and study appropriateness for intended use. However, the list relies primarily on AI-related terminology in public records, omits some authorized devices pending publication, and links to summaries that exclude much application information. The supplied capture’s 1,522 rows therefore describe that table, not the total population of AI-enabled devices. Researchers and buyers should distinguish authorization status from comprehensive evidence access and avoid deriving market-wide conclusions from list coverage alone.

kps.k: Transparency remains a developing governance measure rather than a demonstrated solution to safety or trust problems.
kps.d: FDA’s consultations explored whether transparency could improve safety and effectiveness and what manufacturers should disclose to patients and providers. Its device-list account proposes exploring foundation-model tagging, including LLM and multimodal functionality, and encourages sponsors to supply relevant public-summary information. These are consultation objectives and future methodological plans, not evidence that transparency improved outcomes or that tagging already operates.

qs.q: - To support transparency in the use of modern AI technologies, the FDA will explore methods to identify and tag medical devices that incorporate foundation models encompassing a wide range of AI systems, from large language models (LLMs) to multimodal architectures.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices (AI-Enabled Medical Device List) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: To facilitate the FDA’s development of methods to identify AI-enabled medical devices more easily, including identifying those devices incorporating LLM-based functionality in a future update of this list, sponsors are encouraged to include appropriate information in their public summaries.

vlens.an: Within this curated regulatory voice, the FDA materials accept the proposition that classification and authorization alone are insufficient and materially develop it through operational lifecycle controls. The common rationale is that medical AI is iterative and therefore requires risk-managed change planning, representative data, distinct testing practices and continuing oversight, while public authorization records provide only partial transparency. Material variation lies in function and force: the PCCP guidance supplies a concrete but nonbinding total-product-lifecycle framework for qualifying device software, whereas the device list chiefly supports the proposition by acknowledging incomplete coverage and limited disclosure rather than establishing additional oversight. The materials also frame foundation-model tagging as future work, not an implemented safeguard or demonstrated safety outcome.

qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the principal proposition that regulatory classification cannot substitute for lifecycle oversight. Both treat formal categories as consequential but insufficient: one shows that uncertain FDA boundaries shape development strategy, including efforts to secure clinical-decision-support rather than diagnostic-device classification; the other emphasises clinicians’ independent review and reports proposals for oversight beyond research classification, including continuing data-quality monitoring, algorithm development and validation processes, and patient-data protections. Material variation lies in emphasis: Humans in the Loop focuses on regulatory uncertainty and developers’ responses, whereas Automated Decision Support Technologies and the Legal Profession focuses on human review and enhanced governance conditions. Neither source independently substantiates the synthesis’s additional claims about predetermined change-control plans, representative testing, public-record completeness or transparency outcomes. Because these are curated sources, their agreement should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across academia and research.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the proposition’s core claim that formal classification cannot substitute for continuing human and institutional oversight. It presents two aligned reasons: clinicians should be able to independently review the basis of decision-support recommendations rather than rely primarily on them, and systems may require enhanced ethical and regulatory safeguards even when their use falls outside the Common Rule’s research category. The latter safeguards include conditions of use, ongoing data-quality monitoring, algorithm-development and validation processes, and patient-data protections. The support is nevertheless limited and partly indirect: the excerpt reports statutory language and cited health-care governance proposals rather than clearly offering its own comprehensive framework. It also does not address several material elements of the completed synthesis, including planned modifications, representative testing, distinctions between tuning and performance testing, or the limits of public authorization records. Because only one curated source is supplied for this period, its position should not be treated as representative of wider views during 2015–2022.

elens.an: The selected 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that medical-AI classification is consequential but insufficient, and they materially develop its lifecycle-oversight component. Humans in the Loop supports the diagnosis: FDA boundaries affect whether software is treated as a medical device, remain uncertain for some AI-enabled clinical decision support, and can shape developers’ classification strategies. The FDA guidance goes further by supplying a concrete governance mechanism for qualifying AI-enabled device software: predetermined change control plans grounded in benefit-risk analysis, modification-risk management and a total-product-lifecycle approach, supplemented by representative-data and testing recommendations. Material variation lies in scope and function. Humans in the Loop primarily identifies unresolved boundary questions and strategic responses to them, without presenting a comprehensive oversight framework. FDA provides that framework, but only for software functions qualifying as devices; its guidance is nonbinding, permits legally compliant alternatives and describes potential benefits rather than measured clinical outcomes. These sources therefore build on the proposition without establishing that the framework is effective across all clinical AI or that classification uncertainty was fully resolved.

elens.an: The 2026 FDA device-list source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that regulatory classification and public authorization records cannot replace lifecycle oversight or comprehensive clinical evidence. Its main reason is that authorization-list visibility is intrinsically limited: public summaries omit much of the underlying application material, identification depends primarily on terminology in public records, and the list is expressly noncomprehensive. It also treats foundation-model tagging as planned methodological work rather than an existing safeguard, reinforcing the synthesis’s distinction between developing transparency measures and demonstrated safety oversight. Internal variation is limited but material: the source affirms that listed devices met applicable premarket requirements and presents the list as useful for transparency, innovation and public safety, while simultaneously narrowing what can be inferred from inclusion. It therefore supports rather than opposes regulatory classification, but rejects treating classification or inventory status as sufficient evidence. Because this period contains one curated source, the assessment describes that source only and does not indicate broader prevalence. The source directly addresses public records and emerging transparency measures, but provides little independent evidence on representative testing, professional review or the full lifecycle-governance framework.
